source_text: Πρὸς μὲν οὖν τοὺς ὁμολογοῦντας τὴν πρόνοιαν καὶ τὰς αὐτὰς ἡμῖν παραδεξαμένους ἀρχάς, εἶτα τῶν οἰκείων ὑποθέσεων οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως ἐκπίπτοντας, τοιούτοις χρήσαιτ᾿ ἄν τις λόγοις καὶ πολλῷ πλείοσι τούτων, εἴ γε πλατύνειν ἐθέλοι τὰ συντόμως καὶ κατ᾿ ἐπιδρομὴν εἰρημένα. Πρὸς δέ γε τοὺς περὶ τῶν πρώτων διαφερομένους ἴσως ἂν ἔχοι καλῶς ἑτέραν ὑποθέσθαι πρὸ τούτων ἀρχήν, συνδιαποροῦντας αὐτοῖς περὶ ὧν δοξάζουσι, καὶ τοιαῦτα συνδιασκεπτομένους, ἆρά γε πάντη καθάπαξ ἡ τῶν ἀνθρώπων παρῶπται ζωὴ καὶ σύμπας ὁ βίος, ζόφος δέ τις βαθὺς κατακέχυται τῆς γῆς, ἀγνοίᾳ καὶ σιγῇ κρύπτων αὐτούς τε τοὺς ἀνθρώπους καὶ τὰς τούτων πράξεις, ἢ πολὺ τούτων ἀσφαλέστερον τὸ δοξάζειν ὅτι τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ ποιήμασιν ἐφέστηκεν ὁ ποιήσας, πάντων τῶν ὁπωσοῦν ὄντων ἢ γινομένων ἔφορος, ἔργων τε καὶ βουλευμάτων κριτής. Εἰ μὲν γὰρ μηδεμία μηδαμοῦ τῶν ἀνθρώποις πεπραγμένων γίνοιτο κρίσις, οὐδὲν ἕξουσι πλεῖον τῶν ἀλόγων ἄνθρωποι· μᾶλλον δὲ κἀκείνων πράξουσιν ἀθλιώτερον, οἱ τὰ πάθη δουλαγωγοῦντες καὶ φροντίζοντες εὐσεβείας καὶ δικαιοσύνης ἢ τῆς ἄλλης ἀρετῆς, ὁ δὲ κτηνώδης βίος ἄριστος, ἀρετὴ δὲ ἀνόητος, δίκης δὲ ἀπειλὴ γέλως πλατύς, τὸ δὲ πᾶσαν θεραπεύειν ἡδονὴν ἀγαθὸν τὸ μέγιστον, δόγμα δὲ κοινὸν τούτων ἁπάντων καὶ νόμος εἷς τὸ τοῖς ἀκολάστοις καὶ λάγνοις φίλον Φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν, αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνήσκομεν. Τοῦ γὰρ τοιούτου βίου τέλος οὐδὲ ἡδονὴ κατά τινας, ἀλλ᾿ ἀναισθησία παντελής. Εἰ δέ ἐστί τις τῷ ποιήσαντι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους τῶν ἰδίων ποιημάτων φροντὶς καὶ σώζεταί που τῶν εὖ ἢ κακῶς βεβιωμένων ἡ διάκρισις, ἤτοι κατὰ τὸν παρόντα βίον, ζώντων ἔτι τῶν κατ᾿ ἀρετὴν ἢ κακίαν βεβιωκότων, ἢ μετὰ θάνατον, ἐν χωρισμῷ καὶ διαλύσει τυγχανόντων. Ἀλλὰ κατ᾿ οὐδέτερον τῶν εἰρημένων εὑρεῖν δυνατὸν σωζομένην τὴν δικαίαν κρίσιν· οὔτε γὰρ οἱ σπουδαῖοι κατὰ τὴν παροῦσαν ζωὴν φέρονται τὰ τῆς ἀρετῆς ἐπίχειρα, οὔτε μὴν οἱ φαῦλοι τὰ τῆς κακίας. Παρίημι γὰρ λέγειν ὅτι, σωζομένης τῆς φύσεως ἐν ᾗ νῦν ἐσμέν, οὔθ᾿ ἡ θνητὴ φύσις ἐνεγκεῖν οἷά τε τὴν σύμμετρον δίκην πλειόνων ἢ βαρυτέρων φερομένων πλημμελημάτων. Ὅ τε γὰρ μυρίους ἐπὶ μυρίοις ἀνελὼν ἀδίκως λῃστὴς ἢ δυνάστης ἢ τύραννος οὐκ ἂν ἑνὶ θανάτῳ λύσειε τὴν ἐπὶ τούτοις δίκην· ὅ τε μηδὲν περὶ θεοῦ δοξάζων ἀληθές, ὕβρει δὲ πάσῃ καὶ βλασφημίᾳ συζῶν, καὶ παρορῶν μὲν τὰ θεῖα, καταλύων δὲ νόμους, ὑβρίσας δὲ παῖδας ὁμοῦ καὶ γυναῖκας, κατασκάψας δὲ πόλεις ἀδίκως, ἐμπρήσας δὲ οἴκους μετὰ τῶν ἐνοικούντων καὶ δηϊώσας χώραν, καὶ τούτοις συναφανίσας δήμους καὶ λαοὺς ἢ καὶ σύμπαν ἔθνος, πῶς ἂν ἐν τῷ φθαρτῷ σώματι πρὸς τὴν τούτοις σύμμετρον ἀρκέσειε δίκην, προλαμβάνοντος τοῦ θανάτου τὸ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν καὶ μηδὲ πρὸς ἕν τι τῶν εἰργασμένων τῆς θνητῆς ἐξαρκούσης φύσεως; Οὔτ᾿ οὖν κατὰ τὴν παροῦσαν ζωὴν ἡ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν δείκνυται κρίσις οὔτε μετὰ θάνατον.
thought_title: Judgment must come after death, since it does not come in this life
orientation: Athenagoras has just argued that the corruptible body must put on incorruptibility so that each person may receive what he did through the body; he now turns to those who disagree about first principles and argues that if there is no judgment, human life is worse than that of beasts, but if there is judgment, it cannot be found in this life.
pass_a_gloss: Against those who agree about providence and have accepted the same principles as us, and then somehow fall away from their own assumptions, one might use such arguments and many more than these, if indeed he should wish to expand what has been said briefly and in summary. But against those who differ about first principles, it would perhaps be well to lay down another principle before these, joining with them in perplexity about what they believe, and examining together with them such questions: whether the life of humans has been altogether utterly overlooked and the whole of life, and some deep darkness has been poured over the earth, hiding in ignorance and silence both the humans themselves and their deeds, or whether it is far safer than these to believe that the maker stands over his own works, overseer of all things that in any way exist or come to be, judge of deeds and counsels. For if no judgment anywhere should come to be of the things done by humans, humans will have nothing more than the irrational animals; rather they will fare more miserably than those, those who enslave the passions and care for piety and justice or the rest of virtue, and the beastly life is best, and virtue is foolish, and the threat of punishment is broad laughter, and to serve every pleasure is the greatest good, and the common doctrine of all these and one law is what is dear to the licentious and lustful: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. For the end of such a life is not even pleasure according to some, but complete insensibility. But if there is some care by the maker of humans for his own works, and the distinction between those who have lived well or badly is preserved somewhere, either during the present life, while those who have lived according to virtue or vice are still living, or after death, when they are in separation and dissolution. But according to neither of the things mentioned is it possible to find the just judgment preserved; for neither do the good during the present life receive the rewards of virtue, nor indeed do the bad receive those of vice. For I pass over saying that, while the nature in which we now are is preserved, neither is the mortal nature able to bear the proportionate punishment when more or heavier offenses are brought. For the robber or ruler or tyrant who has unjustly killed ten thousand upon ten thousand would not pay the penalty for these with one death; and the one who believes nothing true about God, but lives with every outrage and blasphemy, and overlooks divine things, and destroys laws, and outrages boys and women alike, and unjustly razes cities, and burns houses with their inhabitants and devastates the land, and with these destroys peoples and nations or even a whole race, how would he in the corruptible body suffice for the punishment proportionate to these, when death anticipates what is according to worth and the mortal nature does not suffice even for one of the things done? Neither therefore during the present life is the judgment according to worth shown, nor after death.

choices.why: The compound verb conveys shared doubt or joint inquiry, matching the author's dialectical strategy of engaging critics on their own ground.

choices.term: ζόφος δέ τις βαθὺς κατακέχυται τῆς γῆς
choices.english: some deep darkness has been poured over the earth
choices.why: The perfect passive of καταχέω suggests a state of darkness spread over the earth; 'poured over' keeps the liquid metaphor and the perfect force.
rejected: a deep darkness covers the earth
deep gloom is spread over the earth

choices.why: The articular participle is used absolutely for God as creator; 'maker' preserves the participial force and avoids importing a proper name.

choices.term: Φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν, αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνήσκομεν
choices.english: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die
choices.why: This is a direct quotation of Isaiah 22:13 as cited by Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:32; the hortatory subjunctives and present indicative are rendered literally.
rejected: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die
Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die

choices.why: The noun denotes lack of sensation or perception; 'insensibility' captures the philosophical sense of a state without feeling, which the author contrasts with pleasure.
The noun means wages or recompense, especially for deeds; 'rewards' fits the contrast with the bad receiving 'those of vice'.

bible_refs.note: Φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν, αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνήσκομεν

pass_b_english: Against those who acknowledge providence and accept the same principles as we do, but then somehow fall away from their own assumptions, one could use arguments like these, and many more besides, if one wished to expand what has been said briefly and in summary. But against those who differ about the first principles, it would perhaps be well to lay down another starting point before these, joining with them in perplexity about their opinions and examining together with them such questions as this: Has human life been utterly overlooked, and the whole of existence, with some deep darkness poured over the earth, hiding in ignorance and silence both human beings themselves and their deeds? Or is it far more certain to believe that the maker stands over his own works, as overseer of all things that in any way exist or come to be, and judge of deeds and purposes?

For if no judgment anywhere ever comes upon what human beings have done, they will have nothing more than the brute animals. Rather, they will fare more miserably than even those. They restrain their passions and devote themselves to piety and justice or the rest of virtue, while the beastly life is best, virtue is folly, the threat of penalty is a broad joke, serving every pleasure is the greatest good, and the common doctrine of all these and their one law is the motto dear to the licentious and lustful: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." For the end of such a life is not even pleasure, as some say, but complete insensibility.

But if the maker of human beings has any care for his own works, and the distinction between those who have lived well or badly is preserved somewhere, then either it happens in the present life, while those who have lived according to virtue or vice are still alive, or after death, when they are in separation and dissolution. But according to neither of these alternatives is it possible to find just judgment preserved. For neither do the good in the present life receive the rewards of virtue, nor do the wicked receive those of vice.

I pass over saying that, if the nature in which we now exist were preserved, mortal nature could not bear a penalty proportionate to the greater number or weight of the offenses committed. For a robber or ruler or tyrant who has unjustly killed thousands upon thousands could not pay the penalty for these things with one death. And one who holds no true opinion about God, but lives in every outrage and blasphemy, neglecting divine things, overthrowing laws, outraging children and women alike, unjustly razing cities, burning houses with their inhabitants, devastating the countryside, and with these things destroying peoples and nations or even a whole race, how could he in a corruptible body suffice for a penalty proportionate to these deeds, when death anticipates what is deserved and mortal nature is not sufficient even for one of the things he has done? So neither in the present life is judgment according to what is deserved shown, nor after death.

problems.why: φερομένων πλημμελημάτων = 'committed/transacted offenses,' not 'brought against it.' The offenses are committed by the person, not brought against nature.
problems.fix: the greater number or weight of offenses committed
problems.ruling: ‘φερομένων πλημμελημάτων’ means offenses committed, not ‘brought against it’, altering agency

problems.why: παρορῶν = 'overlooking/neglecting,' not 'despising.' 'Despising' is stronger; 'neglecting' or 'disregarding' is closer.
problems.ruling: ‘παρορῶν τὰ θεῖα’ means neglecting/disregarding, not despising; stronger tone misrepresents intent

edits.old: the greater number or weight of the offenses brought against it
edits.new: the greater number or weight of the offenses committed

fixed: φερομένων πλημμελημάτων means offenses committed, not brought against nature; changed to 'committed'.
παρορῶν means overlooking/neglecting, not despising; changed to 'neglecting'.

problems.quote: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (1 Corinthians 15:32).
problems.source_quote: Φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν, αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνήσκομεν.
problems.why: The source gives a proverbial saying, not a biblical citation; no book or verse is named.
problems.fix: Remove the parenthetical “(1 Corinthians 15:32)” and keep the proverb without a scriptural reference.

edits.old: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" (1 Corinthians 15:32).
edits.new: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die."

fixed: Removed the parenthetical scriptural citation because the source gives the saying as a proverb without naming any book or verse (Φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν, αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνήσκομεν).

problems.why: κἀκείνων = 'than those' (the animals just mentioned), but English 'those animals' makes wrong comparison.
problems.ruling: ‘κἀκείνων’ refers to the previously mentioned people, not ‘those animals’; English misidentifies referent.

problems.quote: while the nature in which we now exist is preserved
problems.source_quote: σωζομένης τῆς φύσεως ἐν ᾗ νῦν ἐσμέν
problems.why: Ablative absolute: 'if the nature in which we now are were preserved' (unreal condition), not temporal 'while'.
problems.fix: if the nature in which we now exist were preserved
problems.ruling: ‘σωζομένης τῆς φύσεως…’ is a conditional genitive, not a temporal ‘while’; English misstates condition.

problems.source_quote: οὔθ᾿ ἡ θνητὴ φύσις ἐνεγκεῖν οἷά τε
problems.why: Same unreal: 'mortal nature could not bear' (potential in condition).
problems.ruling: ‘οὔθ᾿ ἡ θνητὴ φύσις ἐνεγκεῖν…’ is potential ‘could not bear’; English uses present ‘cannot’, changing meaning.

edits.old: while the nature in which we now exist is preserved, mortal nature cannot bear
edits.new: if the nature in which we now exist were preserved, mortal nature could not bear

fixed: Changed 'than those animals' to 'than even those' because κἀκείνων means 'than even those' (the animals just mentioned), not 'those animals'.

Changed 'while the nature in which we now exist is preserved, mortal nature cannot bear' to 'if the nature in which we now exist were preserved, mortal nature could not bear' because σωζομένης τῆς φύσεως is an unreal conditional (ablative absolute), and ἐνεγκεῖν οἷά τε is potential, not temporal.

problems.quote: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.
problems.why: Reader may not recognize this as Scripture (Isaiah 22:13) or as words of the dissolute; presented as a motto of the lawless.
problems.fix: Signal it as a quotation or motto of the wicked.

edits.old: and the common doctrine of all these and their one law is what is dear to the licentious and lustful: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die."
edits.new: and the common doctrine of all these and their one law is the motto dear to the licentious and lustful: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die."

fixed: The source reads δόγμα δὲ κοινὸν τούτων ἁπάντων καὶ νόμος εἷς τὸ τοῖς ἀκολάστοις καὶ λάγνοις φίλον Φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν, αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνήσκομεν. The English already presents the quotation as the common doctrine and law of the licentious and lustful, which is accurate. The confirmed problem is a style suggestion, not a mistranslation; however, I added 'motto' to make the quotation's status clearer without changing the meaning.

problems.quote: the beastly life is best, virtue is folly
problems.why: Reader cannot tell if these are the author's words or the objector's position.

edits.old: They restrain their passions and devote themselves to piety and justice or the rest of virtue, while the beastly life is best, virtue is folly, the threat of penalty is a broad joke, serving every pleasure is the greatest good, and the common doctrine of all these and their one law is the motto dear to the licentious and lustful:
edits.new: They restrain their passions and devote themselves to piety and justice or the rest of virtue, while they will conclude that the beastly life is best, virtue is folly, the threat of penalty is a broad joke, serving every pleasure is the greatest good, and the common doctrine of all these and their one law is the motto dear to the licentious and lustful:

fixed: The source does not explicitly mark the beastly life/virtue/penalty/pleasure claims as the objectors' conclusion, but the context (if no judgment, humans fare worse than animals) implies these are the consequences drawn by those who deny judgment. The English now introduces them as 'they will conclude that' to clarify the speaker.

refereed.quote: if the nature in which we now exist were preserved
refereed.source_quote: σωζομένης τῆς φύσεως ἐν ᾗ νῦν ἐσμέν
refereed.why: Misreads conditional: not 'if preserved' but absolute participle 'since nature is preserved.'
refereed.fix: since the nature in which we now exist is preserved
refereed.ruling: Greek states nature is preserved (fact), translation adds conditional ‘if’.

polish.changed: Clarified the implied subject of the sentence about restraining passions, broke the long opening question into two clearer alternatives, and kept the quotation as a recognizable motto without adding interpretive gloss.
